in_context.text: Paul charges Timothy to keep his commandment blameless until Jesus Christ appears (6:14). Verse 15 adds that God will bring about that appearing at his own proper time. It then breaks into praise of God as the one true Ruler over every ruler, and the praise continues in 6:16.

speaker.text: Paul the apostle, who names himself as the letter's author. Many critical scholars think a follower wrote in his name.

audience.text: Timothy, Paul's younger co-worker, whom Paul had left to lead the church at Ephesus. Here Paul addresses him as "man of God."

affected.text: The verse speaks about God, the "blessed and only Potentate." It also speaks about all earthly kings and lords, who are ranked beneath him.

what.text: The verse promises that Christ's appearing will be shown "in his times," the times God has fixed. It names God with royal titles: the blessed and only Ruler, King over all who reign, Lord over all who rule.

events.text: The charge is given in Timothy's present, but the appearing it points to is still future. The text does not give a date and leaves the timing to God ("in his times").

written.text: Traditional view: about AD 62-64, between Paul's two Roman imprisonments. Scholarly view: many critical scholars date it around AD 80-110, though others defend the earlier date.

where.text: The letter went to Ephesus, a wealthy port city and capital of the Roman province of Asia. Where it was written from is not stated; it may have been Macedonia.

purpose.text: The praise backs up the charge. Timothy should stay faithful because the one who will bring about Christ's appearing is the supreme Ruler. This comes right after warnings against greed and false teaching.

big_picture.text: The letter praises God in similar words elsewhere: "the blessed God" (1:11) and "the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only wise God" (1:17). The Old Testament also calls the LORD the great King over all the earth.

for_readers.text: The letter was written while Nero was emperor, and the word "king" was commonly used of the Roman emperor. The verse places every human ruler under God.

christians_differ.text: Readers differ over whom the titles describe. One view: they describe God the Father, who will "shew" Christ's appearing and whom "no man hath seen" (6:16). Another view: they also fit Christ, since Revelation gives the same titles to the Lamb.

why_it_matters.text: The word means a fixed, definite time or season. So "in his times" stresses that God has set the timing of Christ's appearing, not people.
This word is also used for human princes and high officials. Calling God the "only" one sets him above every ruler who carries that title.
In Greek the phrase is literally "King of those who reign." It claims rule over everyone who currently holds power.
This is literally "Lord of those who rule as lords." It is a parallel claim of authority over every master.

takeaway.text: The verse is not a stand-alone slogan. It is the reason Timothy should keep faithful until Christ appears: God, the true Ruler over all rulers, will bring that day at his own time.

unsupported.reason: It states as fact that the letter was written under Nero. That follows only the traditional dating. The card's own date source notes that many scholars date the letter to AD 80-110, after Nero's reign.
